resolved_by: Supreme Court, Jones v. Hendrix, 143 S. Ct. 1857 (2023), which held that § 2255(h) does not make § 2255 inadequate or ineffective for a claim based on an intervening change in statutory interpretation
issue: Can a federal prisoner use the saving clause of § 2255(e) to bring a § 2241 petition based on a post-conviction change in statutory interpretation that may mean the conduct of conviction is no longer criminal?

sides.position: The saving clause permits a § 2241 petition when a change in statutory interpretation raises the potential that the prisoner was convicted of conduct the law does not make criminal (the In re Dorsainvil exception).
cases: Trenkler v. United States, 536 F.3d 85 (1st Cir. 2008)
Reyes-Requena v. United States, 243 F.3d 893 (5th Cir. 2001)

sides.position: Section 2255(h)'s limits on second or successive motions mean that § 2255 is not inadequate or ineffective, so a prisoner cannot use § 2241 to raise a post-conviction change in statutory interpretation; the Dorsainvil exception is abrogated.
cases: Steven Voneida v. John Johnson, 88 F.4th 233 (3d Cir. 2023)

this_court: Follows Jones: the saving clause does not permit a § 2241 challenge based on an intervening change in statutory interpretation, and Dorsainvil is abrogated
quote: The Jones decision resolved the circuit split.
cite: Steven Voneida v. John Johnson, 88 F.4th 233 (3rd Cir. 2023)
